blocks.html: Part 1: Proving who is calling · Module 6
JWKS, revocation and introspection
Last reviewed 2026-10-04 · Jump to reference

Objective. After this module you can say which key a verifier will use and why, write down which refresh outcomes are allowed to change what it holds, measure how long a withdrawn grant keeps working, and test the failure states rather than the happy path.

Before you start. Module 5 covers JWT validation and the token profile. This module is the two questions that module deliberately left open: where the verifying key comes from, and what happens when a grant is withdrawn before the token expires.
Published lesson 7 of 35Complete the lesson and quick check, then record your progress.
Learn
1. The attack

Running example: ExampleHotels publishes its signing keys at a JWKS endpoint, and the balance API verifies tokens against them. Company names are fictional.

Module 5's verifier had a key. This module asks where it came from, and the answer is a cache that was filled over the network at some point in the past. That cache is a state machine, and most implementations only ever exercise one of its states.

What happensRefresh only on unknown kidScheduled refresh addedPlus a defined failure policy
A key is rotated in, with an overlapHandledHandledHandled
A key is rotated out after the overlapStill acceptedRejectedRejected
The issuer serves an empty key setStill acceptedRejectedRejected
The endpoint returns a 502 error pageCache silently emptied, or kept, undefinedUndefinedLast known good kept, that request fails
Two keys share one kidFirst one wins, silentlyFirst one winsRejected as ambiguous
A grant is withdrawn before the token expiresAccepted until expiryAccepted until expiryAccepted until expiry
The last row never turns green, because none of it is a key problem. Local validation describes the token, not the grant. That is section 5.
2. Why it works

Three assumptions do the damage.

  • "The cache is a performance detail." It is the thing that decides which keys are trusted. Every refresh outcome is a decision about whether to keep trusting what you hold, and if you never wrote those decisions down, your library made them for you.
  • "A failed refresh and an empty answer are the same thing." They are opposites. A 502 page or a timeout means you learned nothing, so the last known good set should stand. A successful, well-formed set containing no usable signing keys means the issuer just told you something, and ignoring it is how a key that was deliberately withdrawn keeps working. Systems that treat both as "keep what we have" cannot revoke a key. Systems that treat both as "empty the cache" fall over when the endpoint hiccups.
  • "Expiry is revocation." It is not. A self-contained token is a signed statement about the past. Nothing in it changes when the account is disabled. Even a revocation request does not reach every server at once. RFC 7009 section 2.1: "In practice, there could be a propagation delay, for example, in which some servers know about the invalidation while others do not."

The ambiguity case is quieter. RFC 7517 section 4.5 says different keys in a set SHOULD use distinct kid values, and FAPI 2.0 section 5.4.2 says a server "should not serve a JWK set with multiple keys with the same kid". Both are recommendations, so a set with duplicates is malformed-ish rather than illegal, and a verifier that picks the first match will silently accept a token signed by whichever key the issuer happened to list first.
3. The control
Write the state machine down
Six outcomes, and each one needs an answer before you ship. Two of them are project baselines here, because no specification settles them.

refresh outcome                  authoritative?   what the caller sees
-------------------------------- ---------------- --------------------
200, well formed, keys present   yes, replace     verify against the new set
200, well formed, zero keys      yes, replace     reject, nothing verifies
200, malformed or truncated      no, keep         this request fails
non-2xx status                   no, keep         this request fails
transport failure or timeout     no, keep         this request fails
unknown kid after a refresh      n/a              reject, unknown kid

Rows two and three are the pair that matters. Getting them the same way round is the defect. "This request fails" means a request whose kid is not in the set you kept. A request whose kid is in the kept set is still served, until the kept set reaches the staleness limit in step 3 below.
How the verifier resolves a key

1. If the set is older than its maximum age, refresh on your own schedule. Without this, a key the issuer removed keeps verifying for as long as its kid stays in the cache.
  2. If a refresh attempt fails, keep the last known good set and start a back-off. Make no other attempt until it has passed, so a failing endpoint is asked once per back-off, not once per request. Time the back-off from the failed attempt, and keep that time separate from the time of the last successful load, so a healthy endpoint is still refreshed on schedule. While the endpoint is down, a kid in the stale set still verifies. That is a choice: a key the issuer removed lasts for the outage and for up to one back-off after it, unless the next step stops it first.
  3. Set a hard limit on staleness. Once the last successful load is as old as the limit (one hour here), stop serving the set: reject every token, with a reason of its own, until a refresh succeeds. Keep retrying at the back-off rate. Time the limit from the last successful load and test it after the refresh attempt, so a healthy endpoint never reaches it, even after a quiet period. This fails closed. A removed key can no longer outlast the limit, and an outage of the key endpoint longer than the limit becomes an outage of this API for every caller.
  4. Look up the kid from the token header. Use it only to select from keys you already trust; never to fetch anything.
  5. If the kid is missing from the set, allow one bounded refresh, with request coalescing so concurrent misses cause one fetch, and a cooldown so a stream of unknown kid values cannot drive a fetch storm against your issuer.
  6. If two eligible keys share that kid, reject as ambiguous. Do not select by array order.
  7. Check the key is meant for this job: use of sig, and an alg your profile allows. A key published for encryption is not a verification key.
  8. Verify the signature, then apply the module 5 profile in full.
  9. For anything where a withdrawn grant must stop working sooner than the token expires, consult current state as well. That is introspection, a denylist, or a gateway lookup, and it is a separate decision with its own freshness.
The whole system
Untrusted inputServer decisionsCached stateRejection path

Two caches sit on the request path, and each one has its own staleness. The key cache decides which signatures you still trust. The introspection cache decides how long a withdrawn grant keeps working.
4. Defaults and when to change them

DecisionStarting defaultChange it when
Scheduled refreshRefresh the key set when it passes 10 minutes oldYour issuer documents a different rotation cadence. Removing the schedule entirely is what makes a withdrawn key keep working.
Refresh on unknown kidOne bounded attempt, coalesced across concurrent requests, with a 5 minute cooldownNever remove the cooldown. Without it, a stream of invented kid values is a denial of service aimed at your issuer.
Back-off after a failed refreshWait 60 seconds after any failed attempt before the next one, timed from the failure and not from the last successful loadProject baseline, not a specification requirement. A longer back-off spares the issuer and lets a removed key verify for longer once the endpoint is back. Do not reuse the 5 minute cooldown here. Measured in the lab, one failed attempt then keeps a removed key verifying for 899 seconds, against 659 with this default.
Hard limit on stalenessStop serving a key set whose last successful load is one hour old. Reject every token as "key set too stale" until a refresh succeeds, and keep retrying at the back-off rateProject baseline. None of the sources this lesson cites sets a limit on how long a cached key set may be served. Shorten it when a removed key must stop sooner, and keep it well above the maximum age. Lengthen or remove it only under the condition below this table.
Successful set with zero keysAuthoritative. Replace what you hold, and reject everything after itProject baseline, not a specification requirement. If you invert it, write down that a deliberately emptied key set will not take effect.
Malformed or failed refreshNot authoritative. Keep the last known good set, and fail the request that needed the refresh. A request whose kid is in the kept set is still served, even when the set is past its maximum age, up to the staleness limitProject baseline. Inverting it means one bad gateway response logs out every caller. The cost is that a removed key keeps verifying while the endpoint is down, up to the staleness limit, so alert on the outage.
Duplicate kidReject as ambiguousNever select by array order. RFC 7517 and FAPI 2.0 both recommend against publishing duplicates, so treat a set containing them as a fault to report.
Revocation boundA documented number, tested, not an aspirationChoose it from the impact of a compromised token. The number you can defend is the token lifetime plus every cache TTL on the path.
Introspection cachingCache only if you can state the resulting blind windowRFC 7662 allows caching "at the cost of liveness", and requires that a response carrying exp is not cached beyond it.

Why one hour. Two numbers set the range. The limit must sit well above the 10 minute maximum age, because the gap between them is the outage this API rides out with no caller whose key is in the kept set affected: 50 minutes here, which is 50 attempts at the 60 second back-off. That figure assumes steady traffic, so the set is no more than 10 minutes old when the outage starts. The limit is timed from the last successful load, not from the start of the outage, so a verifier that has served no request for an hour rejects from its first failed fetch (measured: last load at 0, endpoint down from 3599 seconds, first request at 3600 seconds rejected). A limit equal to the maximum age turns one failed fetch into a rejection of every caller. And the limit is the whole bound for a removed key during an outage. Token lifetime does not help there, because whoever holds a leaked signing key writes their own expiry. This lab's access tokens live about one hour, so one hour is a window this design already accepts for a stolen token. It is this project's starting point. None of the sources this lesson cites gives a number for it.

Which failure the baseline prefers. Without a limit, anyone who can keep the key endpoint unreachable from the verifier keeps a removed key alive for as long as they can hold the block. With the limit, the removed key stops one hour after the last successful load, and from then on the most the same attacker can do is deny service: every caller is rejected for as long as the block holds. This project prefers the denial of service. It is loud, it accepts no forged token, and it ends when the block ends (measured in the lab: within one back-off). The unbounded key is silent, and what it lets through cannot be taken back.

When a team would choose differently (Option). Where rejecting every caller does more harm than honouring a removed key for the length of an outage, and the path to the key endpoint is hard for an attacker to block, a team may set a much longer limit or none. They then write the outage, with no upper limit, into their revocation bound, and alert on it.
5. What it proves, and what it doesn't

Proves: that the signature was made by a key the issuer publishes now, or published at your last successful load, which is never more than the staleness limit ago, and, if you consult active state, that the grant was live at the moment you asked.

Doesn't prove: that the grant is live now. Every answer you have is as old as the cache it came from.

Your revocation bound is a sum, not a setting. It is an upper limit: the access token lifetime, plus the key cache maximum age where key removal is the mechanism (and, while the key endpoint is failing, the length of the outage and one back-off, up to the staleness limit and no further), plus the introspection cache TTL, plus any gateway or CDN cache in front. Teams quote the token lifetime and forget the rest. Measure it end to end by disabling an account and timing how long a request keeps succeeding, at every layer that answers.
6. Prove it

These are the states a working implementation must get right. Most only ever test the first one:

  • A token signed by the current key, with a cold cache.
  • A token whose kid is not in the cache, where exactly one refresh happens no matter how many requests arrive at once.
  • A second unknown kid inside the cooldown, which must not cause another fetch.
  • A key rotated in during an overlap, where both old and new tokens verify.
  • A key rotated out after the overlap, which must stop verifying without anyone restarting the service.
  • A successful response containing an empty key list.
  • A refresh returning a 502 error page, a truncated body, or a timeout, where the last known good set must survive and the triggering request must still fail.
  • A key endpoint that stays down after the set has passed its maximum age, where any number of requests inside the back-off cause one fetch, for cached and invented kid values alike.
  • The first request after the back-off, which must cause one more attempt.
  • The endpoint coming back with a different key set, where the removed key stops verifying and the new key verifies, without anyone restarting the service.
  • A key endpoint that is still down just before the staleness limit, where a kid in the kept set must still verify.
  • The same outage at the limit, where every token must be rejected with the staleness reason: one signed by a key still in the kept set, and one signed by a key the issuer removed, although the endpoint never came back.
  • Requests past the limit, which must still cause one fetch per back-off and not one per request.
  • The endpoint coming back after the limit, where the first successful refresh must restore service without a restart.
  • A healthy endpoint over several hours, including a quiet period longer than the limit, which must never reject for staleness.
  • A set containing two keys with the same kid.
  • A kid naming a key published with use of enc.
  • A token header carrying jku or x5u, which must change nothing.
  • A grant withdrawn while a token is still within its lifetime, measured at every cache on the path.

Check 11 is the one worth sitting with. The issuer emptied its key set, which is what you would do if a signing key leaked, and the cache honoured it. A verifier that treats an empty set as "nothing to learn here" keeps accepting the compromised key indefinitely, and nothing in its logs looks wrong. Compare it with checks 12 and 14, where the refresh genuinely failed and keeping the old set is the right answer.

Checks 16 to 20 are one outage. The issuer removed a key, and its endpoint went down before the cache learned of it. Check 16 is the cost of keeping the last known good set: the removed key still verifies from a stale set. Check 17 is the back-off: five requests, two of them with invented kid values, cause one fetch. Check 18 is the retry once the 60 second back-off has passed. Checks 19 and 20 are the recovery: the new set replaces the old one, the removed key stops and the new key verifies.

How long can a removed key keep verifying? Measured against this cache with one request a second: 599 seconds after the last successful load when the endpoint is healthy, 659 seconds when one refresh attempt fails, and 1619 seconds through a 1000 second outage that starts as the set goes stale. Those 1000 requests cause 17 fetches. Without the back-off they cause 1000. So the bound is the maximum age, plus the outage, plus one back-off, and the outage is the part you do not control. The staleness limit caps it.

Checks 21 to 25 are a longer outage. The cache holds two keys, the issuer removes one of them, and the endpoint goes down and stays down. Each request carries a token signed at that moment, so token expiry plays no part. Check 21 is 3599 seconds after the load, one second before the limit: the removed key still verifies from the stale set. Checks 22 and 23 are at 3600 seconds, the limit: a key that is still good and the removed key get the same answer, reject: key set too stale, although the endpoint never came back. Check 24 is the back-off past the limit: five requests cause no fetch, because the attempt made at check 21 started a back-off. Check 25 is the recovery: the first attempt after the back-off succeeds and service is restored. Check 26 is a healthy endpoint: 14 requests over four hours, the last after two quiet hours, and none is rejected, because the limit is timed from the last successful load and tested after the refresh attempt.

The new worst case, measured with one request a second: with the endpoint down for good, the removed key last verifies at 3599 seconds after the last successful load, one second short of max_stale. In 72 outage windows tried it never verified at 3600 seconds or later. With the limit removed it was still verifying at the end of a 9000 second sweep. The cost, measured through an outage from 600 to 5000 seconds: a caller whose key was never removed is accepted up to 3599 seconds, rejected from 3600 to 5039 (1440 seconds), and accepted again at 5040, the first attempt after the endpoint is back. The 4400 requests during that outage cause 74 fetches. An outage that is over within 3600 seconds of the last load rejects nobody.

Checks 28, 31 and 32 are the revocation bound made visible: local validation never notices, the introspection cache extends the window by its TTL, and only after that does the token stop working.

Exit 1, seven failures: checks 10, 11 and 19 go from reject: unknown kid to accept, check 18 prints fetches: 1, check 20 prints reject: unknown kid, and checks 25 and 26 print reject: key set too stale. Which key can now not be withdrawn until the set is an hour old?
  • In Part C, on the line that builds the cached resource server, change cache_ttl=300 to cache_ttl=3600 and rerun. Exit 1, one failure: check 32 goes from reject: token not active to accept. State the new revocation bound in seconds, then add the token lifetime to it for the upper limit. This lab's resource server reaches 3599 seconds, not the sum of 7230.
  • In KeyCache, change backoff = 60 to backoff = 0. Exit 1, three failures: check 17 prints fetches: 5, check 18 prints fetches: 6 and check 24 prints fetches: 5. Every request during an outage now reaches the failing endpoint, before the staleness limit and after it.
  • In KeyCache, change max_stale = 3600 to max_stale = 600, the same as max_age. Exit 1, two failures: checks 16 and 21 go from accept to reject: key set too stale. There is no gap left to ride out an outage in. Measured: one failed attempt at 600 seconds now rejects every caller for 60 seconds.
8. Check your understanding

Why is a 502 from the JWKS endpoint treated differently from a 200 carrying an empty key list?

A 502 means you learned nothing, so the safe move is to keep the set you already trust and fail only the request that needed a refresh. An empty 200 is the issuer telling you something. Treating it as a failure means a key the issuer deliberately withdrew keeps verifying, which is the opposite of what was intended.

Two keys in the set share a kid. Your library picks the first and the token verifies. What is wrong?

Which key verified your token is now decided by array order in someone else's document. RFC 7517 and FAPI 2.0 both recommend against publishing duplicates, so a set containing them is a fault at the issuer. Rejecting as ambiguous surfaces it; selecting silently hides it.

Your tokens live 15 minutes and you cache introspection for 5. What is your revocation bound?

Not 15 minutes. The upper limit is 15 minutes for a token issued just before the withdrawal, plus 5 more for the cached introspection answer, plus anything a gateway or CDN holds. This lab's resource server, given those two numbers, stops sooner: a revoked token works for 299 seconds where introspection is consulted and for 899 seconds where validation is local only, because the verifier rejects an expired token before the cache is read. Quote the sum as the limit, and test it rather than calculating it.

Why does an unknown kid need a cooldown rather than just triggering a refresh?

Because the kid comes from the caller. Without a cooldown, an attacker sending tokens with invented key identifiers turns your resource servers into a load generator aimed at your own issuer, and the outage looks like the issuer's fault.

attrs.data-correct-feedback: Correct. A successful, well formed response is the issuer telling you something, including when it contains no keys. Keeping the old set there is how a withdrawn key keeps verifying.
attrs.data-incorrect-feedback: Not quite. A failed or malformed refresh means you learned nothing, so keeping the last known good set is right there. The empty set is the case that must replace what you hold.

Quick check

Which refresh outcome replaces your cached keys?

Your key cache refreshes. Which outcome should replace the keys you currently hold?

Exercises

Change one thing and predict the output

Each exercise edits one place in labs/jwks_lab.py and asks what the run prints. This lab is a state machine, so an edit here can move more than one check. The answers are the real output of each variant.

1. The key set never goes stale

In KeyCache.resolve, replace the staleness test with stale = False, so the only refreshes left are the on-demand ones triggered by an unknown kid.

Which checks change?

Every option, and why
  • Check 9 is a token signed by a key that is still in the set, so it accepts either way. Rotation overlap is not what breaks.
  • Correct. Exit 1, seven failures. Check 10, the old key removed after the overlap, and check 11, a successful empty set evicting the old key, both go from reject: unknown kid to accept. The outage fails with them: check 18 prints fetches: 1 because nothing retries after the back-off, check 19 accepts the removed key after the endpoint is back, and check 20 prints reject: unknown kid because the only refresh left is the on-demand one and it is inside its cooldown. The staleness limit then catches the cache that stopped refreshing: checks 25 and 26 print reject: key set too stale, the second of them on a healthy endpoint. The key the issuer took away keeps verifying tokens until some other request happens to bring an unknown kid and trigger a refresh, or until the set is an hour old and every caller is rejected. This is the whole reason for a scheduled refresh, and check jwks-02 in the Reference layer states it as a requirement rather than an optimisation.
  • Checks 12 and 14 are on-demand refreshes driven by a missing kid, which this edit leaves in place.
  • The on-demand refresh only fires when a kid is missing from the cache. A revoked key's kid is still in the cache, so nothing ever asks.

2. The active-state cache is used without its TTL

In ResourceServer.call, use any cached answer that exists:

if cached:
    active = cached[0]
Which checks change?

Every option, and why
  • Check 32 does change, and so does check 29, which is the more interesting of the two.
  • Checks 30 and 31 accept in the published run as well. A cache that is working looks the same as a cache that never expires, right up to the moment something is revoked.
  • Correct. Exit 1, two failures: both go from reject: token not active to accept. Check 29 is the one worth looking at. Its server has a TTL of zero, which should mean no caching at all, and the published code gets that right because now - stored < 0 is never true. Remove the comparison and a zero TTL becomes an unbounded one, so the active: true recorded before the revocation is reused forever. Check jwks-07 in the Reference layer asks you to state the blind window, and the point of stating it is that it has to be a number.
  • It does, which is why the published run rejects there. A TTL of zero only means no caching while something still compares against it.

3. A duplicate kid keeps one of the two keys

In KeyCache._absorb, stop marking a repeated kid as ambiguous and let the loop fall through, so the later key in the document wins.

What does the run print differently?

Every option, and why
  • It depends entirely on which of the two the loop kept, and in this document it kept the other one. That is the problem: the outcome is decided by document order.
  • Correct. Exit 1, one failure: the reason changes from reject: ambiguous kid to reject: signature check failed. The token is still refused, but only because the key that happened to survive the loop is not the one that signed it. Measured: swap the two entries in that document and the same edited code answers accept, while the published code answers reject: ambiguous kid under either order. A verifier whose answer depends on the order of a JSON array is not deciding anything, which is what check jwks-05 in the Reference layer is about.
  • It does not. A dictionary keyed by kid holds one entry per kid, and that is exactly why the ambiguity has to be recorded rather than resolved.
  • Check 1 uses a kid that appears once, so it is untouched.

4. A malformed refresh replaces the key set

In KeyCache._refresh, treat a malformed document as authoritative: empty the cache and record the load time before returning malformed.

Which check changes?

Every option, and why
  • Check 12 rejects either way. The request that needed the refresh fails whether or not the bad document is absorbed, which is why it hides the change.
  • Correct. Exit 1, one failure: check 13 goes from accept to reject: unknown kid. One malformed response from the key endpoint now takes down every caller holding a valid token, not just the one unlucky request. The lab's stated baseline is that a malformed or failed retrieval is not authoritative, and this is the measurement behind that sentence. Check jwks-01 in the Reference layer asks for every refresh outcome to have a documented and tested answer. The lab tests four of them: keys present, empty, malformed and failed.
  • The transport failure path returns before the malformed test is reached, so those two are unchanged.
  • It does fail, and that is the point of check 13 sitting right after it: the question is what the next request sees.

Reference
Controls
Standard backed by a cited specification. Baseline this project's default, with reasoning above. Option valid depending on the threat model.

• StandardA JWK Set is a JSON object that must have a keys member whose value is an array of JWKs. RFC 7517 section 5.
  • StandardA server providing a jwks_uri endpoint shall serve it only over TLS. FAPI 2.0 section 5.4.2.
  • StandardRFC 7517 section 4.5 recommends that different keys within a set use distinct kid values, and FAPI 2.0 section 5.4.2 recommends against serving a set with multiple keys sharing a kid. Both are recommendations, not requirements.
  • StandardFAPI 2.0 section 5.4.2 recommends against using the jku and x5u JOSE headers.
  • StandardThe use parameter indicates whether a public key is for encryption or for verifying signatures. RFC 7517 section 4.2. The alg parameter is OPTIONAL, section 4.4.
  • StandardA revocation endpoint returns HTTP 200 whether the token was revoked or was already invalid, because "invalid tokens do not cause an error response since the client cannot handle such an error in a reasonable way". RFC 7009 section 2.2.
  • StandardWhere the authorization server supports revoking access tokens, RFC 7009 section 2.1 recommends that revoking a refresh token also invalidates the access tokens issued from the same grant, and warns that "there could be a propagation delay, for example, in which some servers know about the invalidation while others do not".
  • StandardThe introspection active member is a "Boolean indicator of whether or not the presented token is currently active". RFC 7662 section 2.2.
  • StandardAn introspection response may be cached "at the cost of liveness of the information used by the protected resource to make authorization decisions" (RFC 7662 section 2.2), and a response carrying exp must not be cached beyond it (section 4).
  • BaselineRefresh the key set on a schedule once it passes a maximum age, independently of whether any kid is missing.
  • BaselineOn an unknown kid, allow one bounded refresh, coalesce concurrent misses into a single fetch, and apply a cooldown so caller-supplied identifiers cannot drive a fetch storm.
  • BaselineAfter a failed refresh attempt, make no other attempt until a back-off has passed. Time it from the failure and track it separately from the last successful load, so a failing endpoint is not fetched on every request and a healthy one is still refreshed on schedule.
  • BaselineA successful, well formed key set is authoritative even when it contains zero usable signing keys. It replaces what you hold.
  • BaselineA malformed, truncated, non-success or transport-failed refresh is not authoritative. Keep the last known good set, and fail the request that required the refresh. Keep serving the kept set while the endpoint is down, up to the staleness limit, and count the outage and one back-off in the revocation bound.
  • BaselineSet a hard limit on staleness. Once the last successful load is as old as the limit, serve no key from the set and reject every token with a distinct reason until a refresh succeeds, still retrying at the back-off rate. This fails closed: a removed key cannot outlast the limit, and a longer outage of the key endpoint rejects every caller.
  • BaselineReject a kid that matches more than one eligible key rather than selecting by array order, and report it as an issuer fault.
  • BaselineState the revocation bound as a sum of the token lifetime and every cache TTL on the path, and test it by disabling an account and timing the result.
  • OptionUse introspection or a denylist at the resource server when the revocation bound must be shorter than the token lifetime. The cost is a live dependency on the authorization server.
  • OptionServe the stale key set with a much longer limit, or none, where rejecting every caller is the worse failure and the path to the key endpoint is hard for an attacker to block. The cost is that a removed key verifies for as long as the endpoint is unreachable. Write that into the revocation bound and alert on the outage.
  • OptionUse short token lifetimes instead, accepting that the bound cannot go below one lifetime and that the authorization server sees more traffic.
Review checklist items
These are collected into the site checklist.

• Every key set refresh outcome has a documented, tested answer Success with keys, success with zero keys, malformed, non-success status, and transport failure. State which are authoritative and which keep the last known good set.
  • A key removed by the issuer stops verifying without a restart A scheduled refresh exists, not only a refresh on unknown kid. Test rotation out as well as rotation in.
  • The verifying key is never fetched from a location named in the token jku and x5u in the header change nothing. Key locations come from configuration or issuer metadata.
  • An unknown kid cannot drive a fetch storm One bounded refresh, concurrent misses coalesced, a cooldown enforced. A failing key endpoint is asked once per back-off, not once per request. Test with a stream of invented key identifiers, and with the endpoint down.
  • A kid matching more than one eligible key is rejected as ambiguous No selection by array order. Keys are also filtered by use and by the algorithms the profile allows.
  • The revocation bound is documented as a sum and measured end to end Token lifetime plus key cache age plus introspection cache TTL plus any gateway cache. During a key endpoint outage the key cache term can grow as far as the staleness limit, after which every token is rejected. Disable an account and time how long requests keep succeeding.
  • Introspection caching states its blind window A cached response is not used beyond its exp. The window during which a revoked token still works is written down and accepted.
  • Key set retrieval is over TLS with certificate validation, and failures are alerted A key endpoint that has been unreachable for longer than the maximum age is a security event, not just a latency blip.
Sources

• RFC 7517: JSON Web Key (JWK), May 2015. Sections 4.2, 4.4, 4.5, 5.
  • RFC 7009: OAuth 2.0 Token Revocation, August 2013. Sections 2.1, 2.2.
  • RFC 7662: OAuth 2.0 Token Introspection, October 2015. Sections 2.2, 4.
  • FAPI 2.0 Security Profile, section 5.4.2, JSON Web Key Sets, OpenID Final Specification, 22 February 2025.
  • RFC 8725: JSON Web Token Best Current Practices, February 2020. Section 3.8, pairing the verifying key with the issuer.
  • Python 3.14 documentation: Using Python on Windows. Python install manager, Basic use: how the py command picks a runtime when a virtual environment is active.

intro_prose:
Objective. After this module you can say which key a verifier will use and why, write down which refresh outcomes are allowed to change what it holds, measure how long a withdrawn grant keeps working, and test the failure states rather than the happy path.

Before you start. Module 5 covers JWT validation and the token profile. This module is the two questions that module deliberately left open: where the verifying key comes from, and what happens when a grant is withdrawn before the token expires.

sections.heading: 1. The attack
sections.html:
Running example: ExampleHotels publishes its signing keys at a JWKS endpoint, and the balance API verifies tokens against them. Company names are fictional.

Module 5's verifier had a key. This module asks where it came from, and the answer is a cache that was filled over the network at some point in the past. That cache is a state machine, and most implementations only ever exercise one of its states.

What happensRefresh only on unknown kidScheduled refresh addedPlus a defined failure policy
A key is rotated in, with an overlapHandledHandledHandled
A key is rotated out after the overlapStill acceptedRejectedRejected
The issuer serves an empty key setStill acceptedRejectedRejected
The endpoint returns a 502 error pageCache silently emptied, or kept, undefinedUndefinedLast known good kept, that request fails
Two keys share one kidFirst one wins, silentlyFirst one winsRejected as ambiguous
A grant is withdrawn before the token expiresAccepted until expiryAccepted until expiryAccepted until expiry

The last row never turns green, because none of it is a key problem. Local validation describes the token, not the grant. That is section 5.

sections.heading: 2. Why it works
sections.html:
Three assumptions do the damage.

  • "The cache is a performance detail." It is the thing that decides which keys are trusted. Every refresh outcome is a decision about whether to keep trusting what you hold, and if you never wrote those decisions down, your library made them for you.
  • "A failed refresh and an empty answer are the same thing." They are opposites. A 502 page or a timeout means you learned nothing, so the last known good set should stand. A successful, well-formed set containing no usable signing keys means the issuer just told you something, and ignoring it is how a key that was deliberately withdrawn keeps working. Systems that treat both as "keep what we have" cannot revoke a key. Systems that treat both as "empty the cache" fall over when the endpoint hiccups.
  • "Expiry is revocation." It is not. A self-contained token is a signed statement about the past. Nothing in it changes when the account is disabled. Even a revocation request does not reach every server at once. RFC 7009 section 2.1: "In practice, there could be a propagation delay, for example, in which some servers know about the invalidation while others do not."

The ambiguity case is quieter. RFC 7517 section 4.5 says different keys in a set SHOULD use distinct kid values, and FAPI 2.0 section 5.4.2 says a server "should not serve a JWK set with multiple keys with the same kid". Both are recommendations, so a set with duplicates is malformed-ish rather than illegal, and a verifier that picks the first match will silently accept a token signed by whichever key the issuer happened to list first.

sections.heading: 3. The control
sections.html:
Write the state machine down

Six outcomes, and each one needs an answer before you ship. Two of them are project baselines here, because no specification settles them.

refresh outcome                  authoritative?   what the caller sees
-------------------------------- ---------------- --------------------
200, well formed, keys present   yes, replace     verify against the new set
200, well formed, zero keys      yes, replace     reject, nothing verifies
200, malformed or truncated      no, keep         this request fails
non-2xx status                   no, keep         this request fails
transport failure or timeout     no, keep         this request fails
unknown kid after a refresh      n/a              reject, unknown kid

Rows two and three are the pair that matters. Getting them the same way round is the defect. "This request fails" means a request whose kid is not in the set you kept. A request whose kid is in the kept set is still served, until the kept set reaches the staleness limit in step 3 below.

How the verifier resolves a key

  1. If the set is older than its maximum age, refresh on your own schedule. Without this, a key the issuer removed keeps verifying for as long as its kid stays in the cache.
  2. If a refresh attempt fails, keep the last known good set and start a back-off. Make no other attempt until it has passed, so a failing endpoint is asked once per back-off, not once per request. Time the back-off from the failed attempt, and keep that time separate from the time of the last successful load, so a healthy endpoint is still refreshed on schedule. While the endpoint is down, a kid in the stale set still verifies. That is a choice: a key the issuer removed lasts for the outage and for up to one back-off after it, unless the next step stops it first.
  3. Set a hard limit on staleness. Once the last successful load is as old as the limit (one hour here), stop serving the set: reject every token, with a reason of its own, until a refresh succeeds. Keep retrying at the back-off rate. Time the limit from the last successful load and test it after the refresh attempt, so a healthy endpoint never reaches it, even after a quiet period. This fails closed. A removed key can no longer outlast the limit, and an outage of the key endpoint longer than the limit becomes an outage of this API for every caller.
  4. Look up the kid from the token header. Use it only to select from keys you already trust; never to fetch anything.
  5. If the kid is missing from the set, allow one bounded refresh, with request coalescing so concurrent misses cause one fetch, and a cooldown so a stream of unknown kid values cannot drive a fetch storm against your issuer.
  6. If two eligible keys share that kid, reject as ambiguous. Do not select by array order.
  7. Check the key is meant for this job: use of sig, and an alg your profile allows. A key published for encryption is not a verification key.
  8. Verify the signature, then apply the module 5 profile in full.
  9. For anything where a withdrawn grant must stop working sooner than the token expires, consult current state as well. That is introspection, a denylist, or a gateway lookup, and it is a separate decision with its own freshness.

The whole system

Untrusted inputServer decisionsCached stateRejection path

Two caches sit on the request path, and each one has its own staleness. The key cache decides which signatures you still trust. The introspection cache decides how long a withdrawn grant keeps working.

sections.heading: 4. Defaults and when to change them
sections.heading_text: 4. Defaults and when to change them
sections.html:
DecisionStarting defaultChange it when
Scheduled refreshRefresh the key set when it passes 10 minutes oldYour issuer documents a different rotation cadence. Removing the schedule entirely is what makes a withdrawn key keep working.
Refresh on unknown kidOne bounded attempt, coalesced across concurrent requests, with a 5 minute cooldownNever remove the cooldown. Without it, a stream of invented kid values is a denial of service aimed at your issuer.
Back-off after a failed refreshWait 60 seconds after any failed attempt before the next one, timed from the failure and not from the last successful loadProject baseline, not a specification requirement. A longer back-off spares the issuer and lets a removed key verify for longer once the endpoint is back. Do not reuse the 5 minute cooldown here. Measured in the lab, one failed attempt then keeps a removed key verifying for 899 seconds, against 659 with this default.
Hard limit on stalenessStop serving a key set whose last successful load is one hour old. Reject every token as "key set too stale" until a refresh succeeds, and keep retrying at the back-off rateProject baseline. None of the sources this lesson cites sets a limit on how long a cached key set may be served. Shorten it when a removed key must stop sooner, and keep it well above the maximum age. Lengthen or remove it only under the condition below this table.
Successful set with zero keysAuthoritative. Replace what you hold, and reject everything after itProject baseline, not a specification requirement. If you invert it, write down that a deliberately emptied key set will not take effect.
Malformed or failed refreshNot authoritative. Keep the last known good set, and fail the request that needed the refresh. A request whose kid is in the kept set is still served, even when the set is past its maximum age, up to the staleness limitProject baseline. Inverting it means one bad gateway response logs out every caller. The cost is that a removed key keeps verifying while the endpoint is down, up to the staleness limit, so alert on the outage.
Duplicate kidReject as ambiguousNever select by array order. RFC 7517 and FAPI 2.0 both recommend against publishing duplicates, so treat a set containing them as a fault to report.
Revocation boundA documented number, tested, not an aspirationChoose it from the impact of a compromised token. The number you can defend is the token lifetime plus every cache TTL on the path.
Introspection cachingCache only if you can state the resulting blind windowRFC 7662 allows caching "at the cost of liveness", and requires that a response carrying exp is not cached beyond it.

Why one hour. Two numbers set the range. The limit must sit well above the 10 minute maximum age, because the gap between them is the outage this API rides out with no caller whose key is in the kept set affected: 50 minutes here, which is 50 attempts at the 60 second back-off. That figure assumes steady traffic, so the set is no more than 10 minutes old when the outage starts. The limit is timed from the last successful load, not from the start of the outage, so a verifier that has served no request for an hour rejects from its first failed fetch (measured: last load at 0, endpoint down from 3599 seconds, first request at 3600 seconds rejected). A limit equal to the maximum age turns one failed fetch into a rejection of every caller. And the limit is the whole bound for a removed key during an outage. Token lifetime does not help there, because whoever holds a leaked signing key writes their own expiry. This lab's access tokens live about one hour, so one hour is a window this design already accepts for a stolen token. It is this project's starting point. None of the sources this lesson cites gives a number for it.

Which failure the baseline prefers. Without a limit, anyone who can keep the key endpoint unreachable from the verifier keeps a removed key alive for as long as they can hold the block. With the limit, the removed key stops one hour after the last successful load, and from then on the most the same attacker can do is deny service: every caller is rejected for as long as the block holds. This project prefers the denial of service. It is loud, it accepts no forged token, and it ends when the block ends (measured in the lab: within one back-off). The unbounded key is silent, and what it lets through cannot be taken back.

When a team would choose differently (Option). Where rejecting every caller does more harm than honouring a removed key for the length of an outage, and the path to the key endpoint is hard for an attacker to block, a team may set a much longer limit or none. They then write the outage, with no upper limit, into their revocation bound, and alert on it.

sections.heading: 5. What it proves, and what it doesn't
sections.heading_text: 5. What it proves, and what it doesn't
sections.html:
Proves: that the signature was made by a key the issuer publishes now, or published at your last successful load, which is never more than the staleness limit ago, and, if you consult active state, that the grant was live at the moment you asked.

Doesn't prove: that the grant is live now. Every answer you have is as old as the cache it came from.

Your revocation bound is a sum, not a setting. It is an upper limit: the access token lifetime, plus the key cache maximum age where key removal is the mechanism (and, while the key endpoint is failing, the length of the outage and one back-off, up to the staleness limit and no further), plus the introspection cache TTL, plus any gateway or CDN cache in front. Teams quote the token lifetime and forget the rest. Measure it end to end by disabling an account and timing how long a request keeps succeeding, at every layer that answers.

sections.heading: 6. Prove it
sections.html:
These are the states a working implementation must get right. Most only ever test the first one:

  • A token signed by the current key, with a cold cache.
  • A token whose kid is not in the cache, where exactly one refresh happens no matter how many requests arrive at once.
  • A second unknown kid inside the cooldown, which must not cause another fetch.
  • A key rotated in during an overlap, where both old and new tokens verify.
  • A key rotated out after the overlap, which must stop verifying without anyone restarting the service.
  • A successful response containing an empty key list.
  • A refresh returning a 502 error page, a truncated body, or a timeout, where the last known good set must survive and the triggering request must still fail.
  • A key endpoint that stays down after the set has passed its maximum age, where any number of requests inside the back-off cause one fetch, for cached and invented kid values alike.
  • The first request after the back-off, which must cause one more attempt.
  • The endpoint coming back with a different key set, where the removed key stops verifying and the new key verifies, without anyone restarting the service.
  • A key endpoint that is still down just before the staleness limit, where a kid in the kept set must still verify.
  • The same outage at the limit, where every token must be rejected with the staleness reason: one signed by a key still in the kept set, and one signed by a key the issuer removed, although the endpoint never came back.
  • Requests past the limit, which must still cause one fetch per back-off and not one per request.
  • The endpoint coming back after the limit, where the first successful refresh must restore service without a restart.
  • A healthy endpoint over several hours, including a quiet period longer than the limit, which must never reject for staleness.
  • A set containing two keys with the same kid.
  • A kid naming a key published with use of enc.
  • A token header carrying jku or x5u, which must change nothing.
  • A grant withdrawn while a token is still within its lifetime, measured at every cache on the path.

sections.heading: 7. Lab
sections.html:
Download labs/jwks_lab.py. Like module 5 it needs one package:

Install it into a virtual environment, so it does not change the Python the rest of your machine uses:

Windows              macOS and Linux
py -3 -m venv .venv          python3 -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1    source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install cryptography==50.0.1
python labs/jwks_lab.py

Inside an activated environment use python, not py -3. The py command uses an active environment only when you have not asked for a version: "If you are running in an active virtual environment, have not requested a particular version, and there is no shebang line, the default runtime will be that virtual environment" (Python 3.14 documentation, Using Python on Windows, Python install manager, Basic use). Outside an environment, py -3 is still the right command on Windows.

The issuer's key endpoint and the introspection endpoint are stubs in the process, the clock is a variable, and no sockets are opened.

$ python3 labs/jwks_lab.py
key source: RSA generated for this run; keys and tokens never printed

Part A: choosing a key.
 1. token signed by the key in the set          accept
 2. unknown kid, one bounded refresh finds it   accept
 3. unknown kid again, inside the cooldown      reject: unknown kid
 4. no second fetch during the cooldown         pass: fetches unchanged
 5. two keys sharing one kid in the set         reject: ambiguous kid
 6. kid names a key marked use=enc              reject: key not for signatures
 7. jku in the header is ignored                reject: unknown kid

Part B: the cache as a state machine.
 8. initial load, token verifies                accept
 9. rotation overlap, old token still works     accept
10. old key removed after the overlap           reject: unknown kid
11. a successful empty set evicts the old key   reject: unknown kid
12. malformed refresh, the request needing it   reject: key set refresh failed
13. malformed refresh kept the last good set    accept
14. transport failure, the request needing it   reject: key set refresh failed
15. transport failure kept the last good set    accept
16. outage, stale set, kid still in the set     accept
17. 5 requests inside the back-off              fetches: 1
18. back-off over, the next request retries     fetches: 2
19. endpoint back, the removed key              reject: unknown kid
20. endpoint back, the new key                  accept
21. long outage, 1 s before the limit           accept
22. at the limit, a key still in the kept set   reject: key set too stale
23. at the limit, the removed key               reject: key set too stale
24. 5 requests past the limit, in the back-off  fetches: 0
25. endpoint back, service is restored          accept
26. healthy endpoint, 4 hours, 14 requests      accept

Part C: revocation.
27. before revocation                           accept
28. after revocation, local validation only     accept
29. after revocation, active state consulted    reject: token not active
30. first call fills the active-state cache     accept
31. revoked, but inside the cache window        accept
32. the same token once the cache expires       reject: token not active

all lab checks passed

Check 11 is the one worth sitting with. The issuer emptied its key set, which is what you would do if a signing key leaked, and the cache honoured it. A verifier that treats an empty set as "nothing to learn here" keeps accepting the compromised key indefinitely, and nothing in its logs looks wrong. Compare it with checks 12 and 14, where the refresh genuinely failed and keeping the old set is the right answer.

Checks 16 to 20 are one outage. The issuer removed a key, and its endpoint went down before the cache learned of it. Check 16 is the cost of keeping the last known good set: the removed key still verifies from a stale set. Check 17 is the back-off: five requests, two of them with invented kid values, cause one fetch. Check 18 is the retry once the 60 second back-off has passed. Checks 19 and 20 are the recovery: the new set replaces the old one, the removed key stops and the new key verifies.

How long can a removed key keep verifying? Measured against this cache with one request a second: 599 seconds after the last successful load when the endpoint is healthy, 659 seconds when one refresh attempt fails, and 1619 seconds through a 1000 second outage that starts as the set goes stale. Those 1000 requests cause 17 fetches. Without the back-off they cause 1000. So the bound is the maximum age, plus the outage, plus one back-off, and the outage is the part you do not control. The staleness limit caps it.

Checks 21 to 25 are a longer outage. The cache holds two keys, the issuer removes one of them, and the endpoint goes down and stays down. Each request carries a token signed at that moment, so token expiry plays no part. Check 21 is 3599 seconds after the load, one second before the limit: the removed key still verifies from the stale set. Checks 22 and 23 are at 3600 seconds, the limit: a key that is still good and the removed key get the same answer, reject: key set too stale, although the endpoint never came back. Check 24 is the back-off past the limit: five requests cause no fetch, because the attempt made at check 21 started a back-off. Check 25 is the recovery: the first attempt after the back-off succeeds and service is restored. Check 26 is a healthy endpoint: 14 requests over four hours, the last after two quiet hours, and none is rejected, because the limit is timed from the last successful load and tested after the refresh attempt.

The new worst case, measured with one request a second: with the endpoint down for good, the removed key last verifies at 3599 seconds after the last successful load, one second short of max_stale. In 72 outage windows tried it never verified at 3600 seconds or later. With the limit removed it was still verifying at the end of a 9000 second sweep. The cost, measured through an outage from 600 to 5000 seconds: a caller whose key was never removed is accepted up to 3599 seconds, rejected from 3600 to 5039 (1440 seconds), and accepted again at 5040, the first attempt after the endpoint is back. The 4400 requests during that outage cause 74 fetches. An outage that is over within 3600 seconds of the last load rejects nobody.

Checks 28, 31 and 32 are the revocation bound made visible: local validation never notices, the introspection cache extends the window by its TTL, and only after that does the token stop working.

Try next:

  • In KeyCache._absorb, keep the old keys when the new set is empty. Check 11 flips to accept. You have just built the defect this module exists for.
  • In resolve, change if not self.loaded or stale: to if not self.loaded:. Exit 1, seven failures: checks 10, 11 and 19 go from reject: unknown kid to accept, check 18 prints fetches: 1, check 20 prints reject: unknown kid, and checks 25 and 26 print reject: key set too stale. Which key can now not be withdrawn until the set is an hour old?
  • In Part C, on the line that builds the cached resource server, change cache_ttl=300 to cache_ttl=3600 and rerun. Exit 1, one failure: check 32 goes from reject: token not active to accept. State the new revocation bound in seconds, then add the token lifetime to it for the upper limit. This lab's resource server reaches 3599 seconds, not the sum of 7230.
  • In KeyCache, change backoff = 60 to backoff = 0. Exit 1, three failures: check 17 prints fetches: 5, check 18 prints fetches: 6 and check 24 prints fetches: 5. Every request during an outage now reaches the failing endpoint, before the staleness limit and after it.
  • In KeyCache, change max_stale = 3600 to max_stale = 600, the same as max_age. Exit 1, two failures: checks 16 and 21 go from accept to reject: key set too stale. There is no gap left to ride out an outage in. Measured: one failed attempt at 600 seconds now rejects every caller for 60 seconds.

sections.heading: 8. Check your understanding
sections.html:
Why is a 502 from the JWKS endpoint treated differently from a 200 carrying an empty key list?

A 502 means you learned nothing, so the safe move is to keep the set you already trust and fail only the request that needed a refresh. An empty 200 is the issuer telling you something. Treating it as a failure means a key the issuer deliberately withdrew keeps verifying, which is the opposite of what was intended.

Two keys in the set share a kid. Your library picks the first and the token verifies. What is wrong?

Which key verified your token is now decided by array order in someone else's document. RFC 7517 and FAPI 2.0 both recommend against publishing duplicates, so a set containing them is a fault at the issuer. Rejecting as ambiguous surfaces it; selecting silently hides it.

Your tokens live 15 minutes and you cache introspection for 5. What is your revocation bound?

Not 15 minutes. The upper limit is 15 minutes for a token issued just before the withdrawal, plus 5 more for the cached introspection answer, plus anything a gateway or CDN holds. This lab's resource server, given those two numbers, stops sooner: a revoked token works for 299 seconds where introspection is consulted and for 899 seconds where validation is local only, because the verifier rejects an expired token before the cache is read. Quote the sum as the limit, and test it rather than calculating it.

Why does an unknown kid need a cooldown rather than just triggering a refresh?

Because the kid comes from the caller. Without a cooldown, an attacker sending tokens with invented key identifiers turns your resource servers into a load generator aimed at your own issuer, and the outage looks like the issuer's fault.

Quick check

sections.heading: Which refresh outcome replaces your cached keys?
sections.heading_text: Which refresh outcome replaces your cached keys?
sections.html:
Your key cache refreshes. Which outcome should replace the keys you currently hold?

Exercises

sections.heading: Change one thing and predict the output
sections.heading_text: Change one thing and predict the output
sections.html:
Each exercise edits one place in labs/jwks_lab.py and asks what the run prints. This lab is a state machine, so an edit here can move more than one check. The answers are the real output of each variant.

1. The key set never goes stale

In KeyCache.resolve, replace the staleness test with stale = False, so the only refreshes left are the on-demand ones triggered by an unknown kid.

Which checks change?

Every option, and why
  • Check 9 is a token signed by a key that is still in the set, so it accepts either way. Rotation overlap is not what breaks.
  • Correct. Exit 1, seven failures. Check 10, the old key removed after the overlap, and check 11, a successful empty set evicting the old key, both go from reject: unknown kid to accept. The outage fails with them: check 18 prints fetches: 1 because nothing retries after the back-off, check 19 accepts the removed key after the endpoint is back, and check 20 prints reject: unknown kid because the only refresh left is the on-demand one and it is inside its cooldown. The staleness limit then catches the cache that stopped refreshing: checks 25 and 26 print reject: key set too stale, the second of them on a healthy endpoint. The key the issuer took away keeps verifying tokens until some other request happens to bring an unknown kid and trigger a refresh, or until the set is an hour old and every caller is rejected. This is the whole reason for a scheduled refresh, and check jwks-02 in the Reference layer states it as a requirement rather than an optimisation.
  • Checks 12 and 14 are on-demand refreshes driven by a missing kid, which this edit leaves in place.
  • The on-demand refresh only fires when a kid is missing from the cache. A revoked key's kid is still in the cache, so nothing ever asks.

2. The active-state cache is used without its TTL

In ResourceServer.call, use any cached answer that exists:

if cached:
    active = cached[0]
Which checks change?

Every option, and why
  • Check 32 does change, and so does check 29, which is the more interesting of the two.
  • Checks 30 and 31 accept in the published run as well. A cache that is working looks the same as a cache that never expires, right up to the moment something is revoked.
  • Correct. Exit 1, two failures: both go from reject: token not active to accept. Check 29 is the one worth looking at. Its server has a TTL of zero, which should mean no caching at all, and the published code gets that right because now - stored < 0 is never true. Remove the comparison and a zero TTL becomes an unbounded one, so the active: true recorded before the revocation is reused forever. Check jwks-07 in the Reference layer asks you to state the blind window, and the point of stating it is that it has to be a number.
  • It does, which is why the published run rejects there. A TTL of zero only means no caching while something still compares against it.

3. A duplicate kid keeps one of the two keys

In KeyCache._absorb, stop marking a repeated kid as ambiguous and let the loop fall through, so the later key in the document wins.

What does the run print differently?

Every option, and why
  • It depends entirely on which of the two the loop kept, and in this document it kept the other one. That is the problem: the outcome is decided by document order.
  • Correct. Exit 1, one failure: the reason changes from reject: ambiguous kid to reject: signature check failed. The token is still refused, but only because the key that happened to survive the loop is not the one that signed it. Measured: swap the two entries in that document and the same edited code answers accept, while the published code answers reject: ambiguous kid under either order. A verifier whose answer depends on the order of a JSON array is not deciding anything, which is what check jwks-05 in the Reference layer is about.
  • It does not. A dictionary keyed by kid holds one entry per kid, and that is exactly why the ambiguity has to be recorded rather than resolved.
  • Check 1 uses a kid that appears once, so it is untouched.

4. A malformed refresh replaces the key set

In KeyCache._refresh, treat a malformed document as authoritative: empty the cache and record the load time before returning malformed.

Which check changes?

Every option, and why
  • Check 12 rejects either way. The request that needed the refresh fails whether or not the bad document is absorbed, which is why it hides the change.
  • Correct. Exit 1, one failure: check 13 goes from accept to reject: unknown kid. sections.heading: Controls
sections.html:
Standard backed by a cited specification. Baseline this project's default, with reasoning above. Option valid depending on the threat model.

  • StandardA JWK Set is a JSON object that must have a keys member whose value is an array of JWKs. RFC 7517 section 5.
  • StandardA server providing a jwks_uri endpoint shall serve it only over TLS. FAPI 2.0 section 5.4.2.
  • StandardRFC 7517 section 4.5 recommends that different keys within a set use distinct kid values, and FAPI 2.0 section 5.4.2 recommends against serving a set with multiple keys sharing a kid. Both are recommendations, not requirements.
  • StandardFAPI 2.0 section 5.4.2 recommends against using the jku and x5u JOSE headers.
  • StandardThe use parameter indicates whether a public key is for encryption or for verifying signatures. RFC 7517 section 4.2. The alg parameter is OPTIONAL, section 4.4.
  • StandardA revocation endpoint returns HTTP 200 whether the token was revoked or was already invalid, because "invalid tokens do not cause an error response since the client cannot handle such an error in a reasonable way". RFC 7009 section 2.2.
  • StandardWhere the authorization server supports revoking access tokens, RFC 7009 section 2.1 recommends that revoking a refresh token also invalidates the access tokens issued from the same grant, and warns that "there could be a propagation delay, for example, in which some servers know about the invalidation while others do not".
  • StandardThe introspection active member is a "Boolean indicator of whether or not the presented token is currently active". RFC 7662 section 2.2.
  • StandardAn introspection response may be cached "at the cost of liveness of the information used by the protected resource to make authorization decisions" (RFC 7662 section 2.2), and a response carrying exp must not be cached beyond it (section 4).
  • BaselineRefresh the key set on a schedule once it passes a maximum age, independently of whether any kid is missing.
  • BaselineOn an unknown kid, allow one bounded refresh, coalesce concurrent misses into a single fetch, and apply a cooldown so caller-supplied identifiers cannot drive a fetch storm.
  • BaselineAfter a failed refresh attempt, make no other attempt until a back-off has passed. Time it from the failure and track it separately from the last successful load, so a failing endpoint is not fetched on every request and a healthy one is still refreshed on schedule.
  • BaselineA successful, well formed key set is authoritative even when it contains zero usable signing keys. It replaces what you hold.
  • BaselineA malformed, truncated, non-success or transport-failed refresh is not authoritative. Keep the last known good set, and fail the request that required the refresh. Keep serving the kept set while the endpoint is down, up to the staleness limit, and count the outage and one back-off in the revocation bound.
  • BaselineSet a hard limit on staleness. Once the last successful load is as old as the limit, serve no key from the set and reject every token with a distinct reason until a refresh succeeds, still retrying at the back-off rate. This fails closed: a removed key cannot outlast the limit, and a longer outage of the key endpoint rejects every caller.
  • BaselineReject a kid that matches more than one eligible key rather than selecting by array order, and report it as an issuer fault.
  • BaselineState the revocation bound as a sum of the token lifetime and every cache TTL on the path, and test it by disabling an account and timing the result.
  • OptionUse introspection or a denylist at the resource server when the revocation bound must be shorter than the token lifetime. The cost is a live dependency on the authorization server.
  • OptionServe the stale key set with a much longer limit, or none, where rejecting every caller is the worse failure and the path to the key endpoint is hard for an attacker to block. The cost is that a removed key verifies for as long as the endpoint is unreachable. Write that into the revocation bound and alert on the outage.
  • OptionUse short token lifetimes instead, accepting that the bound cannot go below one lifetime and that the authorization server sees more traffic.

sections.heading: Review checklist items
sections.html:
These are collected into the site checklist.

  • Every key set refresh outcome has a documented, tested answer Success with keys, success with zero keys, malformed, non-success status, and transport failure. State which are authoritative and which keep the last known good set.
  • A key removed by the issuer stops verifying without a restart A scheduled refresh exists, not only a refresh on unknown kid. Test rotation out as well as rotation in.
  • The verifying key is never fetched from a location named in the token jku and x5u in the header change nothing. Key locations come from configuration or issuer metadata.
  • An unknown kid cannot drive a fetch storm One bounded refresh, concurrent misses coalesced, a cooldown enforced. A failing key endpoint is asked once per back-off, not once per request. Test with a stream of invented key identifiers, and with the endpoint down.
  • A kid matching more than one eligible key is rejected as ambiguous No selection by array order. Keys are also filtered by use and by the algorithms the profile allows.
  • The revocation bound is documented as a sum and measured end to end Token lifetime plus key cache age plus introspection cache TTL plus any gateway cache. During a key endpoint outage the key cache term can grow as far as the staleness limit, after which every token is rejected. Disable an account and time how long requests keep succeeding.
  • Introspection caching states its blind window A cached response is not used beyond its exp. The window during which a revoked token still works is written down and accepted.
  • Key set retrieval is over TLS with certificate validation, and failures are alerted A key endpoint that has been unreachable for longer than the maximum age is a security event, not just a latency blip.

details.summary: Why is a 502 from the JWKS endpoint treated differently from a 200 carrying an empty key list?
details.html:
Why is a 502 from the JWKS endpoint treated differently from a 200 carrying an empty key list?

A 502 means you learned nothing, so the safe move is to keep the set you already trust and fail only the request that needed a refresh. An empty 200 is the issuer telling you something. Treating it as a failure means a key the issuer deliberately withdrew keeps verifying, which is the opposite of what was intended.

details.summary: Two keys in the set share a kid. Your library picks the first and the token verifies. What is wrong?
details.html:
Two keys in the set share a kid. Your library picks the first and the token verifies. What is wrong?

Which key verified your token is now decided by array order in someone else's document. RFC 7517 and FAPI 2.0 both recommend against publishing duplicates, so a set containing them is a fault at the issuer. Rejecting as ambiguous surfaces it; selecting silently hides it.

details.summary: Your tokens live 15 minutes and you cache introspection for 5. What is your revocation bound?
details.html:
Your tokens live 15 minutes and you cache introspection for 5. What is your revocation bound?

Not 15 minutes. The upper limit is 15 minutes for a token issued just before the withdrawal, plus 5 more for the cached introspection answer, plus anything a gateway or CDN holds. This lab's resource server, given those two numbers, stops sooner: a revoked token works for 299 seconds where introspection is consulted and for 899 seconds where validation is local only, because the verifier rejects an expired token before the cache is read. Quote the sum as the limit, and test it rather than calculating it.
